Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. Q Fever endocarditis is treated with doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (200-600 mg/d) for at least 18 months for native valve endocarditis and 24 months for prosthetic valve endocarditis.2Treatment success is determined by monitoring antibody titers every 3 months.9Absence of a 4-fold decrease in IgG phase I antibody titers and persistence of IgM phase II antibodies after 1 year of therapy is associated with increased mortality rates.3Valve surgery is indicated for patients with acute heart failure, local complications (abscess, false aortic aneurysm, enlarging vegetations), bacterial resistance, or vegetations larger than 10 mm with associated embolic complications such as ischemic stroke.2,3,8 Treatment was initiated with oral doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (600 mg/d). Cardiac FDG PET/CT demonstrated circumferentially increased metabolic activity in the area of the prosthetic valve, suggestive of aortic root abscess (Figure 2). The patient developed intermittent grade 2 AV block. Three weeks after initial presentation, she underwent cardiac aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve. No aortic root abscess was noted during surgery. Vegetations were detected on the explanted aortic valve, and polymerase chain reaction assay of the specimen was strongly positive forC burnetii(1 256 990 copies/mL). At 6-month follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic, C-reactive protein level was normal, andC burnetiiantibody titers had decreased to 1:5120 for phase I IgG and 1:640 for phase II IgG. Treatment with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine is planned for a duration of 24 months.2

Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. Q Fever endocarditis is treated with doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (200-600 mg/d) for at least 18 months for native valve endocarditis and 24 months for prosthetic valve endocarditis.2Treatment success is determined by monitoring antibody titers every 3 months.9Absence of a 4-fold decrease in IgG phase I antibody titers and persistence of IgM phase II antibodies after 1 year of therapy is associated with increased mortality rates.3Valve surgery is indicated for patients with acute heart failure, local complications (abscess, false aortic aneurysm, enlarging vegetations), bacterial resistance, or vegetations larger than 10 mm with associated embolic complications such as ischemic stroke.2,3,8 Treatment was initiated with oral doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (600 mg/d). Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. case_info.explanation: Coxiella burnetiiendocarditis (Q fever endocarditis) B. Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. Q Fever endocarditis is treated with doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (200-600 mg/d) for at least 18 months for native valve endocarditis and 24 months for prosthetic valve endocarditis.2Treatment success is determined by monitoring antibody titers every 3 months.9Absence of a 4-fold decrease in IgG phase I antibody titers and persistence of IgM phase II antibodies after 1 year of therapy is associated with increased mortality rates.3Valve surgery is indicated for patients with acute heart failure, local complications (abscess, false aortic aneurysm, enlarging vegetations), bacterial resistance, or vegetations larger than 10 mm with associated embolic complications such as ischemic stroke.2,3,8 Treatment was initiated with oral doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (600 mg/d). Cardiac FDG PET/CT demonstrated circumferentially increased metabolic activity in the area of the prosthetic valve, suggestive of aortic root abscess (Figure 2). The patient developed intermittent grade 2 AV block. Three weeks after initial presentation, she underwent cardiac aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve. No aortic root abscess was noted during surgery. Vegetations were detected on the explanted aortic valve, and polymerase chain reaction assay of the specimen was strongly positive forC burnetii(1 256 990 copies/mL). At 6-month follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic, C-reactive protein level was normal, andC burnetiiantibody titers had decreased to 1:5120 for phase I IgG and 1:640 for phase II IgG. Treatment with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine is planned for a duration of 24 months.2

Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. Q Fever endocarditis is treated with doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (200-600 mg/d) for at least 18 months for native valve endocarditis and 24 months for prosthetic valve endocarditis.2Treatment success is determined by monitoring antibody titers every 3 months.9Absence of a 4-fold decrease in IgG phase I antibody titers and persistence of IgM phase II antibodies after 1 year of therapy is associated with increased mortality rates.3Valve surgery is indicated for patients with acute heart failure, local complications (abscess, false aortic aneurysm, enlarging vegetations), bacterial resistance, or vegetations larger than 10 mm with associated embolic complications such as ischemic stroke.2,3,8 Treatment was initiated with oral doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (600 mg/d). Cardiac FDG PET/CT demonstrated circumferentially increased metabolic activity in the area of the prosthetic valve, suggestive of aortic root abscess (Figure 2). The patient developed intermittent grade 2 AV block. Three weeks after initial presentation, she underwent cardiac aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve. No aortic root abscess was noted during surgery. Vegetations were detected on the explanted aortic valve, and polymerase chain reaction assay of the specimen was strongly positive forC burnetii(1 256 990 copies/mL). At 6-month follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic, C-reactive protein level was normal, andC burnetiiantibody titers had decreased to 1:5120 for phase I IgG and 1:640 for phase II IgG. Treatment with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine is planned for a duration of 24 months.2

Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. Q Fever endocarditis is treated with doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (200-600 mg/d) for at least 18 months for native valve endocarditis and 24 months for prosthetic valve endocarditis.2Treatment success is determined by monitoring antibody titers every 3 months.9Absence of a 4-fold decrease in IgG phase I antibody titers and persistence of IgM phase II antibodies after 1 year of therapy is associated with increased mortality rates.3Valve surgery is indicated for patients with acute heart failure, local complications (abscess, false aortic aneurysm, enlarging vegetations), bacterial resistance, or vegetations larger than 10 mm with associated embolic complications such as ischemic stroke.2,3,8 Treatment was initiated with oral doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (600 mg/d).
